title: Pop Balloons for Most Coins
statement:
A row of balloons is described by nums; balloon i carries the number nums[i]. You pop the balloons one at a time, in any order you like, until none are left.

Popping a balloon pays left × own × right coins, where own is its number and left and right are the numbers on its current neighbours: the nearest balloons still unpopped on each side. If there is no balloon left on a side, that side counts as 1. After a pop, the two balloons around the gap become neighbours.

Return the most coins you can collect.

examples.why: Pop 4 first while both neighbours are there (2·4·3 = 24), then 2 (1·2·3 = 6), then 3 (3).
Both neighbours are missing and count as 1: 1·5·1.
Pop the middle 4 (9·4·4 = 144), then 9 (5·9·4 = 180), then 4 (20), then 5. Grabbing the largest payout first, 9 for 180, ends at only 284.

hints: Choosing the first balloon to pop is hard to reason about: after it goes, its two neighbours touch and the two sides are no longer independent. Try thinking about the last balloon instead.

Pad the row with a 1 at each end. For an open range between positions i and j, suppose k is the last balloon popped inside it. At that moment its neighbours are exactly i and j. What happens on each side of k before that?
dp[i][j] = max over i < k < j of dp[i][k] + v[i]·v[k]·v[j] + dp[k][j], where dp[i][j] is the best for popping everything strictly between i and j. Fill it by increasing gap j − i.

explain.intuition:
This is interval DP: the table is indexed by a range (i, j) instead of two prefixes. Pad the row as v = [1, ...nums, 1]; the two pads are never popped. Let dp[i][j] be the most coins from popping every balloon strictly between positions i and j, while i and j themselves are still standing. The answer is dp[0][n+1].

Why decide the last balloon, not the first? If you pop k first, its neighbours k−1 and k+1 become adjacent, so later payouts on the left depend on what happens on the right; the subproblems are tangled. If instead k is the last balloon popped inside (i, j), then while everything else between them goes, k stands like a wall. Balloons left of it only ever see neighbours in (i, k) plus the walls i and k; the right side likewise. The two sides are independent, worth dp[i][k] and dp[k][j], and when k finally goes its neighbours are exactly i and j: v[i]·v[k]·v[j]. Try every k, keep the best. Short ranges must be solved first, so fill by increasing gap.
steps: Build v = [1, ...nums, 1] and a table dp of zeros, size (n+2) × (n+2). A range with no balloon inside (j = i + 1) is worth 0.
For gap from 2 to n + 1, and every i with j = i + gap in range:
For each k strictly between i and j: candidate dp[i][k] + v[i]·v[k]·v[j] + dp[k][j]. Store the largest in dp[i][j].
pitfalls: Greedy rules: popping the biggest payout first, or the smallest balloon first. The third example's greedy order makes 284 instead of 349.
Using v[k−1] and v[k+1] as the neighbours of the last balloon. Everything between has already been popped; its neighbours are the range walls v[i] and v[j].
Filling by i from left to right. dp[k][j] for k > i would not be ready. Go by increasing gap, or by i from right to left.

solutions.title: Try every pop order
solutions.idea: Recursively pop each remaining balloon, pay its current neighbours, and continue on the shorter row. Checks all n! orders.

solutions.title: Memoized recursion on the last balloon
solutions.idea: best(i, j) = max over k in (i, j) of best(i, k) + v[i]·v[k]·v[j] + best(k, j), where k is the last balloon popped between the walls i and j.

solutions.title: Interval table, by increasing gap
solutions.idea: The same recurrence filled bottom-up: every range of gap g only needs ranges with smaller gaps.

followups: Return one best popping order, not just the total.
Each pop now pays left + own + right instead of the product. Does the 'last balloon' argument still work?
Where else does 'choose the last operation inside a range' work? (Hint: multiplying a chain of matrices, cutting a stick at marked points.)
